rv.q: “Maybe Happy Ending,” like Pixar at its very best, nourishes the soul in a way few Broadway shows even attempt to do.
Instead, it is utterly enchanting.

That we nonrobots also connect, pair and empower one another to share a too-brief lifetime is the surprising double vision that makes “Maybe Happy Ending” a ravishing addition to the catalog of Broadway nerdicals.

A near-perfect little fable of set-for-the-scrap-heap robots learning to love and knowing whatever happiness they find will be short-lived, Maybe Happy Ending is, of all things, a musical about androids that absolutely brims with humanity.
Will Aronson and Hue Park's adorable show, imported from South Korea, is a golden example of impactful, engaging, original musical theater.
The odd and simple premise of “Maybe Happy Ending” accomplishes something profound, in examining the nature of connection.
The musical, written by Will Aronson and Hue Park, is an offbeat charmer, a sweet-spirited but unsugary romantic fable that taps neatly into the zeitgeist
"Maybe Happy Ending" is an undeniably moving, well-made, adorable musical, and it is a pleasant surprise to see an audience weep at a show about two robots in love.
The whole shebang is quite the slow-burning charmer, honestly, and deserves to be a bit of a sleeper hit.
The power of this doomed love story – all batteries must die eventually – is only slightly dampened by somewhat pedestrian, indistinct musical theater songs, sans a major showstopper.
The musical is both deeply silly and surprisingly moving—a rare combination.
If you find yourself cruising the streamers at night, sipping chamomile tea and searching for Sliding Doors and Sweet November and French Kiss, then Maybe Happy Ending is waiting for you.

Visually, theatrically, and musically, Maybe Happy Ending, directed by Michael Arden with a nuanced delicacy and lightness of touch, is the most original and innovative show on New York’s main theatrical drag this autumn—and it dazzles with subtlety rather than bombast.

'Ending’ is a one-act meditation on love, loss, mortality, and moral responsibility for the digital age delivered with a mix of sharp humor, poignance, and sheer imagination that’s nothing short of breathtaking.
Maybe Happy Ending is a small-scale musical with a big heart in which all the pieces come together beautifully.
This is a very special show; a tender, visionary ode to the space we're able to create and hold for feeling, and the hope that it may continue.
Arden brings that intelligence back to Broadway.
One of the few totally satisfying musicals to come along in many years, Maybe Happy Ending is an instant classic from Will Aronson and Hue Park who should be on the verge of a brilliant career.
It’s the kind of show that’s hardwired to make you cry.

When Claire's charger breaks, she knocks at Oliver's door, launching a reluctant alliance that beep-bloops toward robot love, even in the face of inevitable robot ruination. As sparks fly, Hue Park's refreshingly crisp lyrics float in singable simplicity on Aronson's quirkily soaring melodies that suggest Guettel as video game composer.
an original show, charmingly acted and cleverly staged, with a touching take on love
It’s a jewel of a musical, and a pure ray of sunshine on a dark winter day.
A musical charmer, Maybe Happy Ending offers a delicate, ultimately touching story distinguished by a graceful score and enhanced by fine performances and a beautifully designed production.
Refreshingly original, this story about two robots who, for a brief moment, meet each other halfway, becomes a poignant celebration of finding connections in an ephemeral world.
There’s nothing robotic about this production: it wears its heart on its sleeve and on charm alone, succeeds.
The show was a big hit in South Korea, where it originated; word-of-mouth and the wonders of social media may well do the trick here.
The robot heart of Maybe Happy Ending is fully charged and I hope this show remains unpacking those feelings for a long time coming.
Maybe Happy Ending is a beguiling show whose power sneaks up on you unawares, suggesting a technological future where human virtues may survive even the possible supremacy of machines.
Sometimes good things come in small packages and this gift being given to Broadway this season is a perfect example.
They are better than the script.

cn.t: Critics embrace this original robot love story as a charming, emotionally resonant gem with a lush score and stunning visuals. Criss and Shen shine in this intimate, tearjerking musical that feels refreshingly quiet and heartfelt amid Broadway's bombast.

sg.ra: Belasco was designed by David Belasco as a 'living room' with a shallow depth to support the Little Theater movement's emphasis on actor-audience proximity. Center Orchestra rows B-D sit at the ideal distance (reviewers cite row B as the fourth row from stage at 'perfect distance') with head-on actor views. Mezzanine overhang begins at row J per SeatPlan, so rows BB-H stay clear.

SeatPlan confirms 'The Mezzanine overhang begins at row J, meaning seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Rows J-Q trade top-of-stage visibility for lower prices. Headout and TickPick both flag G-P/F-O center as value picks. Row N's extra legroom offsets the overhang compromise for tall patrons.

SeatPlan: 'Seats at the Left and Right edges suffer from restricted views of the stage,' particularly corner seats in rows B-E. TickPick confirms 'Far Left/Right Orchestra: Angled views may occur.' Historic box configuration and shallow house geometry amplify side-angle distortion.

sg.vl: Aerial sweet spot, skip row A
sg.ra: Mezzanine hangs close and center row C delivers aerial perspective with decent rake. Row A is a common trap: 'Mezzanine row A seat 111 was obstructed view, and the rail literally blocks half of the stage' (Tripadvisor user report). Balcony overhang begins at mezz row C per SeatPlan, so rows A-B stay open-topped but row A's safety bar offsets that benefit.

Headout flags F-H center as the mezzanine value range. Balcony overhang starting at row C means rows E-H sit under it — top of set may be cut. Side mezzanine suffers progressively more restricted angles 'due to stage curvature' (SeatPlan). Acceptable for dialogue-heavy work but not flown spectacle.

Center Balcony 'extends back six rows on a steep rake which provides a bird's-eye-view of the stage' (SeatPlan). Rows B-D balance price and sightline. Distance is the honest tradeoff: AVFMS reviewer on Maybe Happy Ending noted 'the real problem is how far back the balcony is. You'll have to lean forward to see for most of the show.' Row A safety rail can also obstruct.

sg.vl: Up to 1/3 of stage cut off
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'the curve of the section and other features including the Left Boxes may cut off up to a third of the stage at the outside.' Combined with steep rake, distance, and row A rail, side balcony is the worst seat class in the house. Historic 1907 box architecture is the root cause — it cannot be engineered out per production.

vr.q: This is my biggest Broadway recommendation right now, I don't see how anyone could not fall in love with this show.
If you only see one new show from this Broadway season, I really hope it's this one.
This show deserves an audience. I really, really loved it and highly recommend it. 100 minutes. It'll go by quickly. You'll be moved beyond measure. Go see it.
Maybe happy ending is beautiful and heartbreaking. It is an intimate and quirky and hilarious love story with a really lovely, charming music and an absolutely unreal set.
I love this show it's my pick for Best Musical this year I've seen it six times including in Atlanta and I think every single one of you should go see it
there is this organic and urgent groundswell of love and support that we genuinely want to add our voices to

Honestly, the whole experience from the script and the score to the performances and the production value was really enjoyable and somewhat unexpected, with this being a completely original musical not derived from any preexisting IP.
I was bored because I didn't really care about these characters... but I would recommend this show if you are a sentimental person
